title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
hookLine: a widowed Moabite refuses to leave her mother-in-law: your people shall be my people

lines: GO BACK, EACH TO YOUR MOTHER'S HOUSE.
cards: Three widows on a road out of Moab. The book of Ruth opens "in the days when the judges ruled," and it opens small. A famine in Bethlehem.
Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to Moab to find food. He dies there. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth.
About ten years go by, and both sons die too. When Naomi hears there's bread again, she starts for home with her daughters-in-law. On the road she turns around.
Go back, each of you, to your mother's house. I have nothing left to give you.

teach.h: ORPAH KISSED HER; RUTH CLAVE UNTO HER.
teach.b: They weep. Then the two women choose differently: "Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her." Orpah does what Naomi asked.
The story blames neither woman; it simply stays with the harder choice. Clave is the old past tense of cleave, to hold fast.
The King James uses the same word in Genesis, where a man shall leave his father and mother "and shall cleave unto his wife."
Here it's a Moabite holding on to an Israelite, a young widow to an old one with nothing to offer.

teach.h: THE ROAD, THE BED, THE PEOPLE, GOD.
teach.b: Naomi tries once more, and Ruth answers with the lines this day is named for: "Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
Hear how it climbs. The road. The bed.
The people. God. Then she keeps going: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried.

teach.h: ALL THE WAY TO THE GRAVE.
teach.b: A whole life, and a grave in a foreign country. When Naomi sees she's steadfastly minded, she stops arguing.

teach.h: CALL ME MARA. I CAME HOME EMPTY.
teach.b: In Bethlehem, as the town comes out to look, Naomi says, "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." And: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty."
Empty, with Ruth standing right beside her. Some readers hear a grief so deep it doesn't count her. Ruth stays anyway.
The chapter ends at the start of barley harvest, which matters tomorrow.

how: Christians read Ruth's vow as a picture of faithful love that crosses family, nation and grief, a love that holds on when the other person has stopped hoping.

s: Ruth's well-known vow is spoken to her husband
her husband has died. she speaks it to Naomi, her mother-in-law, on the road.
the text condemns Orpah for going back
Orpah kisses Naomi and goes, as Naomi asked. the story just stays with Ruth.
back in Bethlehem, Naomi says the LORD brought her home empty
Ruth 1:21, with Ruth standing beside her.

games.q: you're Ruth. your husband is dead. your mother-in-law, old and poor, tells you to go back to your mother's house in Moab. what do you do?
o: kiss her goodbye and go home.
refuse: whither thou goest, I will go.
go with her as far as the border, then decide.
games.why: Ruth clave unto her, and vowed to go, lodge, live, worship, die and be buried where Naomi did (Ruth 1:16–17).

practice: Let one person come to mind who is carrying a loss right now, a death, a divorce, a job, their health, maybe bitter, maybe not noticing who's still around.
Hold them in mind without needing thanks, since nobody in this chapter thanks Ruth, and think of one way to stay close: a call, a meal, sitting with them. If you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Naomi. The widowed mother-in-law Ruth refused to leave, who later renamed herself Mara, bitter, after losing everything and returning to Bethlehem empty.

orig.note: Hebrew: clave, held fast. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clave unto Naomi.

carryVoice: Your line: where you go, I go. Ruth took the harder road. See you tomorrow.
